Everything in this universe works under the command of Allah obeying laws which are referred as laws of nature. These laws are hidden and are therefore mysteries for mankind. Human being is the outstanding and best among all creatures of Allah and has been gifted with many qualities. One of these qualities is the curiosity of mankind. It is human nature to try to understand about the working of things and events in his surroundings. He wants to know the origin of universe and the laws governing it. How days and nights are formed? How different seasons are formed? What did go inside the Sun to make it hot? What is the cause of solar and lunar eclipses? How do plants grow? Why do objects fall to the ground? The list of such queries is countless, Man has always tried to understand all these phenomena by logical reasoning. 1.1. WHATIS SCIENCE? The knowledge gained through observation and experimentation is termed. as science. The word ‘science’ has its origin in Latin word 'scientia’ which means knowledge. Initially this knowledge was studied under a single heading called 'natural philosophy’ because of its limited contents. This situation prevailed till the end of seventeenth century. Industrial revolution took place in the eighteenth century and rapid growth in science and technology was also observed. With the passage of time the volume of knowledge about science increased many folds justifying its division into two main branches i.e., physical sciences and biological sciences. Physical Sciences Physical sciences deal with the study of non-living things. Physical sciences are further divided into main five disciplines i.e., Physics, Chemistry, Astronomy, Geology and Meteorology. These disciplines have no well-defined boundaries and this division is made in order to facilitate scientists for study. Physics is present at the roots of every field of science and provides a picture of the world which is continually changing. Biological Sciences Biological sciences deal with the study of living things. Botany, Zoology and Microbiology are the main disciplines of biological sciences.

1.2 INTRODUCTION TO PHYSICS Physics is derived from Greek word 'physikos' meaning the science of natural things. Physics is defined as the study of matter, energy and their mutual interactions. Physics is also considered as the study of the properties of matter, space and time. Physics is further divided into branches to facilitate its study. 1.2.1 Branches of Classical Physics Classical Physics deals with principles developed in many areas of Physics before 20th century and are given below as branches of classical Physics. Each branch of Physics has become so vast that it can be treated as a separate subject. Mechanics It deals with the study of motion of material objects with or without reference of the forces. Heat / Thermal Physics It deals with the nature of heat, mechanisms of heat transfer and its effects on matter. Thermodynamics It deals with conversion of heat energy into other forms of energy (i.¢., mechanical, electrical or chemical energy etc.) or vice versa. Optics It deals with the nature, production, propagation of light and phenomena related to it (i.e., reflection, refraction, interference, diffraction and polarization etc.). The working and use of optical instruments such as camera, microscope and telescope etc. is also studied. Electricity and Magnetism / Electromagnetism It deals with the study of the charges which are either at rest or in motion, their effects and their relationship with magnetism. Electromagnetism is the study of phenomena and laws relating electricity and magnetism. Atomic Physics It deals with the study of structure and properties of atoms. Acoustics The branch of Physics that deals with study of sound (i.c., infrasonic, audible sound and ultrasonic), its production, control, propagation, detection and other related phenomena is called acoustics.

1.2.2 Branches of Modern Physics The developments made in 20th century are studied under the heading of ‘Modern Physics’ and its various branches are listed as under. Nuclear Physics: It deals with the study of structure, properties and reactions of nuclei of atoms. Solid State Physics It deals with the study of physical properties of solid materials. It is also called as ‘Condensed Matter Physics’. Semiconductor Physics It deals with study, design and use of devices based on behaviour of electrons in semiconductors. Low Temperature Physics It deals with production of extremely low temperature and study of properties of matter at low temperatures. It is also known as ‘Cryogenics’ derived from the Greek meaning ‘producing cold’. Quantum Mechanics It deals with the study of matter, electromagnetic radiation and their interactions based on quantum theory. Particle Physics It deals with the study of elementary particles of the nucleus. Plasma Physics It deals with the study of production and properties of the ionic state of matter i.e., nuclei without electrons. Plasma is also referred as the fourth state of matter. 1.2.3 Interdisciplinary Fields Science is a collaborative field that requires interdisciplinary researchers working together to share knowledge and critique ideas. The influence of Physics is observed in every walk of life. The interaction of Physics with other sciences such as Astronomy, Biology, Chemistry and Geology ete. has evolved interdisciplinary fields. This list of such subjects is continuously growing and a few selected subjects are given below. Astrophysics It deals with the study of Physics involved in the study of universe i.e., the properties and interaction of heavenly or celestial objects.

Biophysics It deals with use of Physics in the study of biological processes. Chemical Physics It deals with study of chemical processes from the point of view of Physics. Geophysics It deals with the study of internal structure of Earth. Medical Physics It deals with application of Physics in diagnosis, prevention and treatment of various diseases. The familiar examples are X-rays, ultrasound, CT scan ete. Other Branches of Physics The following branches of Physics are taught at graduate and post-graduate level. Classical Mechanics The study of three equivalent formulation of mechanics as given by Newton, Lagrange and Hamilton is called classical mechanics. Relativistic Mechanics The study of motion of objects moving with velocity comparable with velocity of light using relativistic laws is called relativistic mechanics. Usually, it involves the motion of sub-atomic particles. Computational Physics Computational Physics is defined as study of Physics problems using numerical analysis. Computer programming is also used to solve more complex problems involving large data. Cosmology Cosmology is a branch of Astronomy that deals with the study of the origin, evolution and structure of the Universe. Climate Physics The study of physical processes that regulate Earth's climate system is called ‘Climate Physics'. It involves the study of atmosphere, meteorology, oceans, cryosphere (ice) and biosphere ete. 1.3. IMPORTANCE OF PHYSICS In Physics we study a wide range of phenomena associated with objects as small as sub-atomic particles and as large as galaxies. Physics plays an important role in our daily life and development of science and technology. Radioactivity, electric cars,

submarines, aeroplanes, refrigerator, microwave oven, television, computers, computer tomography (CT scan), magnetic resonance imaging, laser surgery, solar energy panels, mobiles are a few selected applications of Physics. 1.4 WHOIS PHYSICIST? Ascientist who specializes in the research of Physics is called Physicist. A further classification is made depending on the area of specialization within physics. 1.5 HYPOTHESIS, THEORY AND LAW Hypothesis It is defined as the possible explanation of specific observable natural phenomenon based on simplified postulates assumptions or axioms which may be true or untrue. A hypothesis requires further scientific observations and research in order to establish whether the postulates are true or not. The hypothesis may change significantly with more observations. The special theory of relativity is based on two postulates. Bohr model of hydrogen atom is also based on certain postulates. You will study these topics in higher classes. Theory When a hypothesis is tested multiple times with positive results then it is given the name of theory. A theory about a natural phenomenon is more certain than a hypothesis, The atomic theory describes the nature of matter and is supported by experimental evidence. Similarly, the description of large-scale movement of inner layers of the Earth is given by plate tectonic theory. The studies about earthquakes, volcanoes and rocks under sea floor etc. provide evidence about plate tectonic theory. Law A relation among different parameters of a phenomenon which has been found empirically true and applicable in all cases is called a law. The examples are Newton's laws of motion, Newton’s law of universal gravitation, Coulomb's law and laws of radioactivity etc. 1.6 FALSIFIABILITY OF A SCIENTIFIC | a? The items in the list are usually expressed in terms of kilogram. You measure mass in kilogram. Milk, juices, petrol and other liquid items are sold in litres. The height ofa person is expressed in metres. How long it takes you to reach your school from the house? This duration is expressed in terms of seconds, minutes and hours etc. Thus, we are quite familiar, in our daily life, with physical quantities and their units. A physical quantity is defined as under. A quantity which can be measured and expressed in terms of standard units is called a physical quantity.

Length, area, volume, mass, density, time, temperature, speed, force and pressure etc. are examples of physical quantities. A number of physical quantities such as length, mass, time and temperature etc. can be measured directly i.e., they do not depend on other quantities. On the other hand, certain quantities depend on other quantities and cannot be measured directly. Force is defined as the product of mass and acceleration. The measurement of force involves the measurement of two physical quantities i.e., mass and acceleration. Similarly, momentum is defined as the product of mass and velocity. Thus, the measurement of momentum involves the measurement of two quantities namely mass and velocity. A physical quantity is represented by a number followed by is proper unit. This number represents the size or magnitude of the physical quantity with a proper unit. The number alone is meaningless. For example, if mass ofan object is 10 kilograms, then 10 is anumber that gives the size or magnitude of the quantity while kilogram is the unit of mass. Similarly, we express certain length as 15 metres, where 15 is a numerical magnitude and metre is a unit of length. Thus, a physical quantity can be expressed as a numerical value with an appropriate unit. It may be pointed out that laws of Physics are expressed in terms of physical quantities. 2.1.2 Non-Physical Quantity Consider the quantities like colour, taste, smell, happiness and pain etc. You can feel these quantities but cannot express them in terms of standard units like metre, kilogram, second etc. Such a physical quantity does not have magnitude of itself. The quantities given above are examples of non-physical quantities. A quantity which cannot be measured and cannot be expressed in terms of standard units is called a non-physical quantity. 2.2 Types of Physical Quantities Physical quantities are classified into following two groups (i) Base quantities and (ii) Derived quantities. 2.2.1 Base Quantities The physical quantities in terms of which other physical quantities can be measured are called base quantities. These quantities are seven and are independent of one another. The base quantities are length, mass, time, current, temperature, amount of substance and intensity of light. 2.2.2 Derived Quantities The quantities which can be derived from base quantities are known as derived quantities. A derived quantity can be obtained by multiplication or division of either one or more than one base quantities with another base quantity or more than one base quantities. Area, volume, speed, acceleration, force, pressure, work and power ete. are

examples of derived quantities. Observe that the derived quantity ‘area' involves one base physical quantity ‘length’ twice i.e., in the form of product of length and width. Similarly, speed is obtained by dividing one base physical quantity ‘length or distance’ with another base physical quantity ‘time’. Derived quantities can be obtained by combination of (i.e., multiplication or division) of two or more than two base quantities. 2.3. INTERNATIONALSYSTEM OF UNITS Measurement of physical quantities is very common in our daily life. If we say that mass of Physics book is 0.2 then it will make sense only if its units are given i.e., 0.2kg. The measurement of a physical quantity will be meaningful only if it is expressed in proper units. In past, different units were used to measure same physical quantities in various countries. For example, the length was expressed in inches, foot, yard and mile etc. In these systems the conversion of bigger units into smaller units or vice versa was quite complicated and time consuming. The need for a universal system of units was realized to facilitate the growing international collaboration and trade. The International System of Units (from the French Le System International of d'Unites, with the internationally accepted abbreviation SI) is the modern version of the metric system. This was recommended by the 11th General Conference of Weights and Measures held in Paris in 1960. This is widely used system of measurements in science, engineering and technology throughout the world. The conversion of bigger units into smaller units is quite simple and straight forward because it involves multiplication or division by ten (10) or powers of ten. There is no need to specify the direction. The examples of scalar quantities include mass, distance, time, temperature, speed, volume, density, work, energy and power etc. The magnitude of such quantity can be expressed by a number with the proper unit. For example, the distance between two points on ground is 20 m. Here 20 represents the magnitude and m is the SI unit of distance. Scalar quantities can be added, subtracted, multiplied or divided by using usual arithmetical laws. 2.6.2 Vector Quantity A quantity which is completely specified by its magnitude as well as direction is called a vector quantity. You are asked to move five steps. Do you think that this message contains full information? The message is not clear because it does not specify the direction i.e., in the forward, backward, right or left side of the person... However, if direction is mentioned then message is clear. Thus, displacement is a vector quantity. Other examples of vector quantities include velocity, acceleration, force, weight, momentum, torque, electric field and magnetic field etc. A vector quantity becomes meaningful only if its magnitude is expressed by a number with a proper unit and its direction is also specified. Consider an example of a truck which is travelling on a straight flat road which is heading towards North. If the truck travels a distance of 20 km, then 20 km towards North represents its displacement. Similarly, if the weight of an object is 500 N, then it represents a force of 500 N (magnitude) with which the object is attracted by the Earth towards its centre (direction). For example, the diameter of metallic wire as measured by a micrometer screw gauge is 2.65 mm, then there are three significant figures and the last digit 5 is uncertain or doubtful. The precision of a measured value of a physical quantity is given by significant figures. This is illustrated by the following example. Tf 127 mm and 25 mm represent the length and width of a rectangle, the calculated value of area of the rectangle is 127 x 25 = 3175 mm’. We know that the last digit in cach measurement is uncertain. In other words, length could be anything from 126 mm to 128 mm and width could be anything from 24 mm to 26 mm. Thus, area of rectangle lies between 126 x 24 = 3024 mm‘ and 128 x 26 = 3328 mm’. The number of significant figures in length are three and number of significant figures in width are two. Thus, the final answer for area should have two significant figures i.e., 3200 mm” or 3.2 x 10° mm’, The retaining of the final answer to two significant figures ensures that no additional significant figure is introduced due to multiplication (or division) process. All measurements of physical quantities are subject to uncertainties or errors i.e., they are not accurate or exact. The uncertainty or error denotes the limiting accuracy ofa measurement and depends on the following factors. (a) The quality of the measuring instrument. (b) — The skill of the person using that instrument. (c) | Thenumber of observations recorded for the same parameter.

The least count of a metre rod, Vernier calliper and screw gauge are | mm, 0.1 mm and 0.01 mm respectively. A measuring tape will be used to measure the length and width ofa plot of land. Similarly, the thickness of a glass slab or diameter of a metallic wire will be better estimated using screw gauge. You will observe that uncertainty in reading will be different in each case. It depends on the type and quality of measuring instrument. The number of digits shown in this reading is beyond the limit of Vernier callipers. Hence skill of the person using a measuring instrument also plays a vital role in measurement and can minimize the error in reading. Ifmore than one reading are taken for the same parameter i.e., length or diameter ofacylinder then average of these readings will give you a value closer to true value. The number of significant figures is the number of digits whose values are known with certainty. 2.12.1 Rules for Identifying the Number of Significant Figures The following rules are followed in identifying the number of significant figures in a given number or measured quantity. (1) Allnon-zero digits are significant i.e., they are counted. For example 98765 has five significant figures. 1.23 has three significant figures. (2) Allzeroes between two non-zero digits are significant. For example 5401 has four significant figures. 12.005 has five significant figures. (3) All zeroes to the left of first non-zero digits are not significant. For example 0.005 has only one significant figure. 0.067 has two significant figures.

Observe that such zeroes simply indicate the position of the decimal point. (4) Allzeroes to the right ofa decimal point (after the first non-zero digit) are significant. For example 0.0530 has four significant figures. 0.700 has three significant figures. (5) Ifa whole number i.e., a number without a decimal point which ends in one or more zeroes then these zeroes are not necessarily significant. For example 540 may have two or three significant figures. 20300 may have three, four or five significant figures. The above ambiguity can be avoided by expressing the given number in scientific notation i.e., 2.03 x 10° has three significant figures. 2.030 x 10° has four significant figures. 2.0300 x 10° has five significant figures. When two or more numbers / measurements are used in a calculation, the number of significant figures in the final answer will be controlled by the number of significant figures in the original measurements. The number of significant figures in the final answer will not exceed to the smallest number of significant figures in any one of the original number. Precision refers to how closely two or more measurements of the same quantity agree with one another i.e., diameter of cylinder on present case. Precision can be expressed as the difference between value of an individual measurement of a physical quantity and the value of arithmetic mean for successive or repeated measurements of the same quantity. Thus, Precision = Value of the individual measurement — Value of arithmetic mean It is obvious from above word equation that the greater will be the precision of a measurement if above difference is small. We also call precision as repeatability and reproducibility. The precision can be improved by increasing the number of measurements of the same physical quantity. In this case, the value of arithmetic mean

will become close to value any individual measurement. In other words, the precision will be high if scattering of experimental values is small from their mean value. Example Consider a rectangular box whose actual or true value of length is 10.7 em. A large number of measurements of length of rectangular box are made and we can write the length of rectangular box as under. Length of rectangular box = 10.7cm+0.2cm It is clear that the length of the rectangular box lies between 10.5 cm and 10.9 cm. This range reflects that the precision in the measurement of length of rectangular box. 2.13.2 Accuracy Accuracy refers to how close a measurement of a physical quantity is to its true (or accepted) value. Accuracy can be expressed as the difference between experimental value and true or accepted value ofa physical quantity. Thus, Accuracy = Experimental Value —True Value Accuracy is also defined as a measure of degree of conformity. The accuracy of measurement of a physical quantity also depends on the type of device or instrument being used. If we measure the thickness of a glass slide using a Vernier calliper and a screw gauge then micrometer will provide more accurate reading. The concept of accuracy is not useful if the true or accepted value of physical quantity to be measured is not known. In such case, the concept of precision is preferred. 2.13.3 General Remarks Precision of measurement of a physical quantity can only determined if we take several measurements of the same quantity. Accuracy of measurement ofa physical quantity can be determined witha single measurement of the quantity. A measurement of a physical quantity may be precise but not necessarily accurate. A measurement of a physical quantity may be accurate but not necessarily precise.

It may be pointed out that there is a limit to speed that can be achieved by a material object. According to the theory of relativity, there is a universal speed limit for any object in the universe that is approximately 3 x 10°ms"'i.e., speed of light in vacuum or air. A material object cannot exceed this value of speed. Most of the objects move with a speed that is extremely small as compared to speed of light. CENTRIPETAL FORCE When a body moves in a circle with constant speed, then the magnitude of the velocity remains same but its direction is continuously changing. Thus, according to Newton's second law of motion there must be a force acting on the body that changes

the direction of the velocity to keep the body moving in the circle. This force is known as centripetal force (centre seeking force i.e., the force directed towards the centre). The centripetal force is the force which keeps the body to move in the circle and is always directed towards the centre. INTRODUCTION Work and energy are not two different things, but they are correlated to each other. When work is done by one system on another, indeed energy is transferred between the two systems. For example, when an engine pulls a train along a horizontal track, the engine does work. The engine transfers energy to the train. If we assume that there is no loss of energy, then the amount of energy of the moving train is equal to the work done. Similarly, when we walk upstaifs, we do work; our work is equal to gain in gravitational Potential Energy (P.E). Energy is present in the universe in various forms, It ¢an be converted from one form into other form but neither be created nor be destroyed. This is the principle of conservation of energy. For example, a heat engine vonverts heat energy into mechanical energy. A fan converts electrical‘energy into mechanical energy, a bulb converts electrical energy into light and,heat energy etc. All forms of energy can be explained in terms of kinetic energy or’potential energy. These two are the most important types of energies. The Kinetic Energy (K.E) is due to motion while P.E is a stored energy. Here a question arises, how much work is done or how much energy is consumed? It is measured in terms of rate of doing work or rate of consumption of energy which is called power. For example, a boy may carry a box upstairs in 3 minutes while a man maydo it in 1 minute. Obviously, the power of the man is more than the’ power of the boy. Thus, time factor is important for power. A body which has the capacity to do work is said to possess energy. The greater the capacity of the body to do.work, the greater is the energy possessed by it. Thus work, energy and power are rélated.to each other.
